meta.title: "It's cool", "it's for the smart kids" — and your child already agrees, without checking | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to separate appealing wording from the actual substance. Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child agree just because it "sounds convincing"?
hero.subheadline: "It's cool." "It's for smart people." "It's for us." Words create a feeling — and the child reacts to that feeling before ever checking what's actually behind them.

media.alt: A child reacting to how something is said, not to what it means

pain.title: When the wording sounds more convincing than the substance
pain.body:
"It's cool" → and they already want it. "It's the right thing" → and arguing feels embarrassing. "It's for smart people" → and the child is afraid of looking stupid. At school, in ads, in everyday conversation — the same thing can be phrased in different ways, and each phrasing triggers a different reaction.

This isn't being gullible or naive. The child reacts naturally to how something is said: appealing words create a feeling, and the feeling runs ahead of any checking. The substance behind them may be empty — but the wording has already done its job.

The result — decisions get made under the influence of words, not real facts. The child agrees, buys, refuses — not because they worked it out, but because it "sounded good".

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices when they're being convinced by wording, not by facts
🧠 Asks themselves: "what exactly was said — and is there anything real behind it?"
💬 Separates "how it sounds" from "what it actually means"
🛡️ Doesn't decide under the spell of appealing words — checks the substance first

social_proof.quote: "It's cool" or "it's for grown-ups" used to work every time. Now my daughter calmly asks: "But what does that actually mean?" — and sees for herself when there's nothing behind the words.
social_proof.author: Natalia, mum of 11-year-old Katya

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
